T1.fact: Thrust must be greater than weight for liftoff; as propellant burns, rocket mass falls and acceleration increases, so a rocket starts slowly and goes faster as it climbs.
T1.title: Rocket Principles

T2.fact: Thrust-to-weight must be greater than 1 to lift off; as propellant burns the rocket gets lighter so the same thrust gives growing acceleration; staging drops empty tanks so a lighter vehicle takes over.
T2.title: Rocket Propulsion

T3.fact: A satellite stays in orbit by falling around Earth: gravity pulls it in while sideways speed keeps it missing the surface; circular speed is about 7.7 km/s at 400 km and gravity there is still about 89% of surface gravity.
T3.title: How Do Satellites Stay in Orbit? Physics Explained

T4.fact: At 100 km the air is far too thin for wings to lift a craft; above there a vehicle is held up by orbital motion rather than by air, and 99.99997% of the atmosphere lies below 100 km.
T4.title: Karman Line: Where Space Begins (100 km)

T5.fact: Too slow, and a spacecraft spirals back down into the atmosphere; too fast, and it flies off into a higher, more elongated orbit; in a circular orbit distance and speed stay constant.
T5.title: What Is Orbital Velocity and How Satellites Stay in Orbit

T6.fact: Kepler's third law: the square of orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis; higher orbits are slower and take longer, and higher altitude increases the geometric horizon and footprint.
T6.title: Orbital Mechanics FAQ: How Satellites, Orbits, and SSA Actually Work

T7.fact: Higher altitude means a longer orbital period under Kepler's third law; lower altitudes allow higher spatial resolution, while higher altitudes cover a larger area with each pass.
T7.title: Sun-synchronous orbit altitude selection for specific mission requirements

T8.fact: The rocket equation gives speed gain as exhaust velocity times the natural logarithm of full mass divided by empty mass; in the NASA Glenn example about 90% of launch weight is propellant and payload is only about 1%.
T8.title: The rocket equation explained: why reaching orbit takes so much fuel

T9.fact: On the way back a craft starts at full speed and uses friction from air molecules like brakes to slow down; reentry friction can heat a shuttle to more than two thousand degrees Fahrenheit, and heating depends on speed and air thickness.
T9.title: Reentry Heat

T10.fact: A returning craft compresses air ahead of it into a shock layer reaching thousands of degrees; that is why reentry capsules are blunt rather than pointed, pushing the shock layer away from the structure.
T10.title: Why Do Spacecraft Get So Hot During Reentry?

T11.fact: A Hohmann transfer places a craft in an elliptical transfer orbit tangential to both the lower and higher circular orbits; the first burn adds energy and raises the apoapsis, and a second burn at apoapsis raises the periapsis to match the larger circular orbit.
T11.title: Hohmann transfer orbit

T12.fact: A transfer orbit is a long ellipse whose perigee is as low as low orbit and whose apogee is as high as the target orbit; at apogee the satellite fires to make the orbit circular, and each burn at perigee raises the apogee.
T12.title: Types of Satellite Orbits: LEO, MEO, GEO, Polar and SSO

T13.fact: The maximum acceleration of the space shuttle is about 3 g, meaning astronauts feel a force three times their body weight, pushed back into their seats; acceleration is kept under a limit for crew health and safety.
T13.title: Problem 19: The maximum acceleration of the space shuttle

T14.fact: By cutoff, shuttle astronauts felt about three times their normal weight pressing them into their seats; the instant thrust stops, the sensation flips to floating freely, often within a single second.
T14.title: How Long Does It Take to Get to Space in a Rocket?

T15.fact: Earth's escape velocity at sea level is 11.186 km/s, and escape velocity is always exactly the square root of two (about 1.41) times the circular orbital velocity at the same altitude.
T15.title: Escape Velocity Calculator

T16.fact: A spacecraft must reach about 11 kilometres per second to break free of Earth's gravity, and the time to travel to the Moon is approximately 3 days; the Moon is 384,400 km from Earth.
T16.title: How Fast Rockets Must Travel To Reach Orbit Or Escape Earth's Gravity Entirely

T17.fact: A rocket sent away from Earth at escape speed slows gradually under gravity, its speed falling step by step as it climbs away from Earth.
T17.title: What's the point of Escape Velocity?

T18.fact: A recovered vehicle is inspected for heat and stress damage, worn parts are replaced, and it is cleaned and tested before another launch; reuse saves money only when recovery and refurbishment cost less than building new.
T18.title: How Reusable Rockets Work: Landing and Reflight

T19.fact: Reuse saves money only if recovery, inspections and refurbishment cost less than building a new vehicle; flying the same hardware often spreads its build cost across more flights.
T19.title: How reusable rockets cut the cost of reaching space

T20.fact: A sun-synchronous orbit crosses the equator at the same local solar time on every pass, keeping sunlight angle consistent so images from the same season can be compared without extreme shadow/lighting changes.
T20.title: Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits

T21.fact: The SSO plane turns eastward about 0.9856 degrees per day, in step with Earth around the Sun; a dawn-dusk orbit stays in sunlight for nearly the whole year.
T21.title: What Is a Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO)?

T22.fact: Pockets of air bend starlight and blur images; the atmosphere absorbs much ultraviolet and infrared light, so space opens wavelengths the ground cannot see.
T22.title: Space Telescopes: Why We Put Observatories in Orbit

T23.fact: Above the atmosphere an orbiting telescope produces much finer detail than a ground telescope, and can observe ultraviolet and infrared light blocked by the atmosphere.
T23.title: Hubble Space Telescope

T24.fact: Dedicated rideshare flights carry many small payloads on one rocket, with operators paying for a slice instead of chartering a dedicated launch.
T24.title: How Has the SpaceX Transporter Program Reshaped Satellite Earth Observation?

T25.fact: Rideshare satellites get staggered deployment to precise and individual orbits, even when flying as a rideshare.
T25.title: Electron Payload User Guide v8.0

T26.fact: Rendezvous requires matching orbit, velocity and position; a chaser in a lower orbit has higher orbital velocity and catches up, then rises to the target orbit.
T26.title: Space rendezvous

T27.fact: Speeding up raises a craft into a higher, slower orbit; the final docking approach is at only a few centimetres per second relative speed.
T27.title: How Space Rendezvous Works: The Engineering Behind the Maneuver

T28.fact: At 35,786 km above the equator a satellite circles once per Earth rotation and seems to hang in one place; a radio signal takes about a quarter of a second to go up and come back down.
T28.title: Geostationary orbit: why satellites seem to stand still

T29.fact: A geostationary satellite is about 36,000 km up; the up-and-down radio delay is 0.24 seconds, about a quarter of a second.
T29.title: 5.3 Signal speeds, propagation times and distance: the formula triangle

T30.fact: Astronauts float because station, crew and contents fall together around Earth; gravity at that height is still about 90% of surface strength; the station constantly falls toward Earth but moves sideways fast enough to keep missing the ground.
T30.title: Why Astronauts Float: The Real Reason for Weightlessness

T31.fact: Weightlessness is free fall: gravity still acts, but no support force pushes up, so everything accelerates together and seems to float.
T31.title: Apparent Weightlessness in College Physics I

T32.fact: The Moon has no atmosphere, so there is nothing to slow a spacecraft and no air for parachutes; rockets lower the probe all the way down, and lunar gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's.
T32.title: Why India's Chandrayaan-3 moon landing is a big deal

T33.fact: The lunar near-vacuum eliminates aerodynamic braking or parachutes; surface gravity is about 1.62 m/s2, or one-sixth of Earth's, and soft landing requires fully powered descent.
T33.title: Moon landing

T34.fact: A gravity assist uses a planet's motion and gravity to alter a spacecraft's path and speed, typically to save propellant; it can increase or decrease speed.
T34.title: Gravity assist

T35.fact: A spacecraft borrows some of a planet's orbital motion to gain speed without burning fuel; the planet is slowed by an immeasurably small amount.
T35.title: Gravitational Slingshot: How Did Gravity Assist Voyager 1 & 2?

T36.fact: Recovery requires enough remaining propellant to slow the vehicle before touchdown, plus careful inspection between flights; reserving fuel for landing leaves less propellant for accelerating its payload.
T36.title: Reusable Rockets and Launch Systems

T37.fact: Propellant saved for landing reduces payload delivered to orbit; recovered vehicles are inspected and refurbished before flying again.
T37.title: What Is a Reusable Rocket? Booster Reuse Explained

T38.fact: Radio travels at the speed of light, about 299,792 km/s; a signal to the farthest probe takes more than 22 hours one way, and its weak signal needs colossal antennas to catch.
T38.title: A History of Deep Space Communications

T39.fact: The Deep Space Network's largest dishes span 70 metres; a far probe's signal is whisper-weak (about a billionth of a billionth of a watt) and data rates fall as distance grows.
T39.title: How We Talk to Spacecraft

takes.text: Thrust must beat weight, or the rocket never leaves the pad.
A rocket lifts off only when thrust is stronger than weight.
As propellant burns away, the rocket grows lighter and quicker.
Same push, less mass: the rocket speeds up more each second.
Height alone is not orbit; sideways speed is the secret.
To stay up there, a craft must race sideways, not just climb.
Orbit needs sideways speed, so rockets lean over as they climb.
Up here the air is too thin for wings to lift anything.
A satellite never stops falling; it just keeps missing Earth.
Gravity pulls it down while speed bends its path around Earth.
Too slow and it sinks; too fast and it flies farther out.
In a circle, speed and gravity stay in perfect balance.
Higher orbits take longer to circle Earth just once.
A bigger loop means a slower lap around the planet.
From higher up, one view covers far more ground below.
Closer views show fine detail; wider views show whole storms.
Most of a rocket is propellant, not metal or cargo.
Nine parts in ten can be propellant on a trip to orbit.
Speed grows from the ratio of full mass to empty mass.
Dropping empty tanks lets the rest speed up far more easily.
Returning is the hard part; speed must be shed with care.
Air can brake a craft, but fast air turns speed into heat.
Thin air above slows a craft gently before the thick air.
A blunt shape spreads heat wide, shielding what sits behind it.
A push at the low point lifts the high point higher.
Speed up low down, and the far side of the path rises.
The path stretches into a long loop between two circles.
A second push at the far point rounds the path again.
Crew rides stay gentle, near three times Earth's gravity.
At three times your weight, lifting an arm feels heavy.
Crews feel each push as weight pressing them into seats.
When the push stops, the crew floats free at once.
Escape takes about eleven kilometers per second from Earth.
That is more than a third again the speed for a low orbit.
The Moon is days away, along a curved path, not straight up.
Gravity slows the craft the whole way, yet it still arrives.
A flown rocket gets checked top to bottom before its next flight.
Crews look for heat marks, cracks, and worn parts each time.
Sharing one build across many flights can cut the cost per flight.
Reuse pays only when checks and fixes cost less than new.
A sun-synchronous orbit crosses the equator at the same morning hour.
Its path turns slowly, keeping step with the Sun through the year.
Matching shadows let pictures from different days compare cleanly.
A dawn-to-dusk path can stay in sunlight nearly the whole year.
Moving air bends starlight, so stars twinkle and pictures blur.
Above the air, a telescope sees steadier, sharper starlight.
Air blocks much ultraviolet and infrared light from space.
In space, a telescope can catch light the air hides.
Many small satellites can share one ride to orbit.
Sharing a ride spreads the cost across many teams.
Small satellites are released from their carrier one by one.
Each small satellite then follows its own path in orbit.
To meet a station, a visitor must match its orbit exactly.
A lower orbit is faster, so a visitor catches up from below.
Speeding up lifts a craft higher, where it moves slower.
At the end, two craft meet at almost no relative speed.
Thirty-six thousand kilometres up, a satellite matches Earth's spin.
From the ground, that satellite seems to hang over one spot.
A signal takes about a quarter of a second there and back.
A fixed dish can stay aimed at that still satellite.
Astronauts float because their craft falls around Earth with them.
Gravity is still there, pulling at about nine-tenths strength.
With no floor pushing up, floating feels like having no weight.
Orbit is a long fall that keeps missing the ground.
The Moon has almost no air to slow a landing craft.
With no air, parachutes cannot catch anything and slow it.
Rockets must do the braking, firing against the fall.
Lunar gravity is about one-sixth of the pull on Earth.
A passing planet can lend a craft speed, like a slingshot.
The craft curves around the planet and leaves on a new path.
The craft borrows motion from the planet, which barely slows.
The same trick can also slow a craft down, if needed.
A returning rocket saves propellant for slowing down and touching down.
Saving propellant for landing leaves less for lifting cargo.
After landing, crews inspect the rocket before a later trip.
Checked parts can be reused, saving the cost of building new ones.
Radio waves travel at light speed, the fastest possible pace.
Even at that speed, a far probe may answer hours later.
Giant dishes on Earth must track a whisper-quiet signal.
The farther the probe, the weaker and slower its messages grow.
